materials.passage: The willow project opened in the spring. Volunteers met every Monday at the willow office. The first survey recorded ten public routes near the willow. The team stored its paper notes in a locked cupboard marked willow. An independent editor checked each willow report before publication. The willow project closed on Sundays. The willow coordinator trained new volunteers in pairs. Each willow route was checked twice before the map was released. The printed willow maps were distributed free of charge. A local library preserved the final willow report. The willow team treated its archive as a record of decisions rather than a list of isolated observations. Members described where each note had come from, checked the date against the shared timetable, and asked a second reader to inspect unclear entries. This routine made the eventual report easier to trace. Visitors could compare the summary with the original notebooks and understand why a route appeared on the map. When an entry was incomplete, the group left a clear gap instead of filling it with an assumption. The next visit then addressed that gap with a specific question.
